Analyst
-------
  [critical] Red lost R6 on a broken buy: the loss bonus had escalated far enough to fund a real buy, but the team still walked in on a force.
           rule: analyst.pivotal_broken_buy, 5 feature row(s) cited
  [warning] Red went into the pivotal R6 already 2 rounds into a losing streak -- the round that decided the match was played on bonus money.
           rule: analyst.pivotal_streak, 4 feature row(s) cited
  [warning] Red was simply out-fought in the pivotal R6, taking only 33% of the round's kills (sim-approx: kill share stands in for real trade windows).
           rule: analyst.pivotal_trade_collapse, 4 feature row(s) cited
  [warning] Red got the spike down but could not hold it -- only 11% of its plants converted into round wins.
           rule: analyst.post_plant_conversion, 2 feature row(s) cited

           rule: analyst.trade_efficiency, 14 feature row(s) cited

           rule: analyst.pivotal_round, 4 feature row(s) cited

Economist
---------
  [critical] Red broke its buy 4 times (R2, R6, R10, R12) -- rounds where the escalated loss bonus should have funded a real buy and the team went in short anyway.
           rule: economist.broken_buy_count, 4 feature row(s) cited
  [warning] Red force-bought in 5 of 14 rounds (36%), past the 30% mark where forcing stops being a read and starts being a habit.
           rule: economist.force_buy_frequency, 14 feature row(s) cited
  [warning] Red was out-spent by Blue by 1670 credits across the match's 14 rounds -- roughly a third of a full team buy in equipment Red never got to bring.
           rule: economist.spend_disadvantage, 14 feature row(s) cited

provenance.detail: val-match-v1 requires a Riot production key. Matches here are generated by an in-repo simulator that emits payloads in the documented val-match-v1 shape, grounded in real agent and map UUIDs fetched live from val-content-v1. Nothing is scraped and no unofficial API is used. Every module downstream of the match adapter is source-agnostic, so live data swaps in with no code change.
provenance.note: Simulated data conforming to the val-match-v1 schema — production key application pending
provenance.proxy_note: Momentum index, not a calibrated win probability: a bounded logistic over score state and round spend differential. It ranks rounds against each other within one match and says nothing about the odds of winning.
provenance.sim_approx_note: Kill share stands in for trade efficiency: the simulator emits no death timestamps, so real trade windows cannot be detected.

conclusions.claim: Red lost R6 on a broken buy: the loss bonus had escalated far enough to fund a real buy, but the team still walked in on a force.
Red broke its buy 4 times (R2, R6, R10, R12) -- rounds where the escalated loss bonus should have funded a real buy and the team went in short anyway.
Red went into the pivotal R6 already 2 rounds into a losing streak -- the round that decided the match was played on bonus money.
Red was simply out-fought in the pivotal R6, taking only 33% of the round's kills (sim-approx: kill share stands in for real trade windows).
Red got the spike down but could not hold it -- only 11% of its plants converted into round wins.
Red was out-traded across the match, taking 37% of round kills over 14 rounds against a 50% even split (sim-approx: kill share stands in for real trade windows).
Red force-bought in 5 of 14 rounds (36%), past the 30% mark where forcing stops being a read and starts being a habit.
Red was out-spent by Blue by 1670 credits across the match's 14 rounds -- roughly a third of a full team buy in equipment Red never got to bring.
R6 was the match's pivotal round -- the largest single swing (0.141) in the win-probability proxy. Blue took it, Red lost it.
Blue stole 1 of its 1 eco rounds (100%).
Red stole 0 of its 1 eco rounds (0%).
